communityVoices.quote: The Sugaree is, in my opinion, nothing less than the most brilliant and inspired version of this incredible tune.
30 plus years supporting this band and (Dare I say) maybe, wasting a good bit of my life or a lot of time and potential. But...no regrets
this one doesn't have a single let down...not one note
The ending medley is one of the first things from '77 i ever heard, and it couldn't be more perfect.
As consistently good as anything from 1977.

whyThisShow: This is a canonical May '77 show, released on Dick's Picks Vol. 29 alongside 5/21/77, and the community broadly treats it as the peak of that already-peak month. One listener, cross-referencing the Deadhead's Compendium, called it the "Best show of May 77" and noted it "doesn't have a single let down...not one note" [source: 'this one doesn't have a single let down...not one note']. Another goes further, calling 5-19-77 "the best of the best" among May '77 shows and placing it at "the Dead's technical and artistic peak" [source: '5-19-77 is indeed the best of the best']. The Sugaree alone accounts for a lot of that reputation — one reviewer described it as carrying "three separate, distinct jams, all of which could stand alone and still be amazing" [source: 'It has three separate, distinct jams, all of which could stand alone and still be amazing']. The second set closing sequence drew its own devotees, with one listener saying the ending medley "couldn't be more perfect" as an entry point into '77 [source: "The ending medley is one of the first things from '77 i ever heard, and it couldn't be more perfect."].
listenFor: Start with the Sugaree — it runs around 20 minutes and one reviewer described it as "the sweetest 20 or so minutes of listening pleasure" built from three distinct jams that collectively constitute something beyond any single one of them [source: 'collectively they constitute the sweetest 20 or so minutes of listening pleasure']. The Peggy-O and Row Jimmy are also flagged as highlights, with one listener noting "the way Jerry switches back and forth from normal lead guitar playing to slide guitar is unfathomable" across those two songs [source: 'the way Jerry switches back and forth from normal lead guitar playing to slide guitar is unfathomable']. One reviewer specifically pointed to "Second set's Terrapin through the conclusion of Playin" as showing "stunning cohesion between the band members" [source: "Second set's Terrapin through the conclusion of Playin is just stunning cohesion between the band members"]. The recording is a soundboard, so the detail is there to hear all of it clearly.
context: This show was recorded at the Fox Theatre in Atlanta on May 19, 1977, deep in the era widely regarded as the band's creative and technical peak. The recording circulates as a clean soundboard (identifier: gd77-05-19.sbd.direwolf.3120.sbeok.shnf). It was officially released by the band's organization as Dick's Picks Vol. 29, paired with the May 21, 1977 show — the organization's endorsement of both nights as representative of the era. Note: some Archive reviews from the mid-2000s reflect a period when officially released shows were temporarily pulled from free streaming, which generated commentary unrelated to the music itself.
funFact: One reviewer noted a peculiar guitar texture on the Playing Reprise — describing Garcia producing "a bass like underwater kind of sound" for roughly the first three minutes while "Keith and Phil don't play for a while" — and asked if anyone had heard that sound from Garcia's guitar before [source: 'Garcia starts a unique sounding with a bass like underwater kind of sound. Keith and Phil don\'t play for a while and its just Garcia with this bass like underwater sound'].
headline: Fox Theatre Sugaree, May '77, three jams deep.
